message.content:
The sea was a hammer against the cliffs, and Elias, the lighthouse keeper, was its anvil. He’d been at his post for forty years, a solitary man whose heart beat in time with the great lamp’s slow, revolving pulse. His world was a spiral of light, a rhythm of oil and brass, and the endless, whispering conversation of the waves.

One night, a storm unlike any other descended. The wind screamed, and the rain was a solid, stinging wall. Through the glass, Elias saw a sight that chilled his marrow: a fishing boat, a tiny, broken toy, being hurled toward the jagged teeth of the rocks. He knew the drill. He grabbed the heavy foghorn and gave three long blasts, a sound that was swallowed whole by the tempest.

He saw a figure on the deck, waving a frantic lantern. It was useless. The rocks were too close. Elias felt a profound, ancient grief; he was a witness, not a savior. He watched as the boat struck, splintering like a matchstick. The light in his tower blazed on, indifferent to the tragedy below.

Hours later, the storm passed. The sea, exhausted, lay flat and gray under a weak dawn
